topics.title: The one idea underneath everything
topics.detail: Think in sets of employee rows. Describe the result grain first, such as one row per active employee, and let the optimizer choose the access path.

topics.title: Tables, rows, and the relational model
topics.detail: A table represents a relation with named columns. A primary key identifies each employee and foreign keys express relationships such as reports-to-manager.

topics.title: The logical processing order of a SELECT
topics.detail: Reason through FROM and JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, and then pagination. That explains why a SELECT alias usually cannot appear in WHERE.

topics.title: Logical order is not physical order
topics.detail: Logical order defines the result. SQL Server can push filters down and reorder compatible joins where the transformation preserves that result.

topics.title: Client–server: the cost you forget
topics.detail: An HR dashboard that requests attendance individually for 100 employees can burn 100 round trips. Compare one grouped request with the per-employee implementation.

topics.title: ACID in one page
topics.detail: Atomicity groups related writes, consistency preserves declared rules, isolation constrains what parallel transactions observe, and durability preserves committed changes.

topics.title: Chapter summary
topics.detail: Before tuning a query, name its result grain, candidate keys, filters, and ordering. These tell you what the rewrite must preserve.

chapters.title: The Schema Used in This Book

topics.title: Entity overview
topics.detail: The PDF uses banking entities. The HRMS lab uses employees, attendance shifts, leave entries, and payroll components, with employees at the center.

topics.title: Data definition
topics.detail: Open the sample schema and trace the primary and foreign keys. Each attendance, payroll, or leave row references an employee. The manager relationship references the same employee table.

topics.title: Reading the DDL like an engineer
topics.detail: Read data types, nullability, CHECK rules, and keys as business constraints. A nullable manager can represent the CEO. A nullable attendance employee would make the shift impossible to attribute.

topics.title: Seeding sample data
topics.detail: Seed parent employees first, then their detail records. Include split shifts, tied payroll totals, missing attendance, and dates on both sides of a month boundary.

chapters.title: Data Types and the Truth About NULL

topics.title: Choosing types deliberately
topics.detail: Use a DATE for calendar dates and DECIMAL or integer cents for payroll. SQLite represents this lab’s dates as sortable ISO strings. SQL Server can enforce native date types.

topics.title: NULL is not a value
topics.detail: NULL represents an unknown or absent value. WHERE manager_id IS NULL finds employees with no manager. Equality with NULL produces UNKNOWN.

topics.title: How aggregates treat NULL
topics.detail: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(manager_id) counts known manager IDs. SUM and AVG ignore NULL inputs and yield NULL when there are no non-NULL inputs.

topics.title: Handling NULL: COALESCE, ISNULL, NULLIF
topics.detail: COALESCE can choose among several expressions. T-SQL ISNULL takes two and usually keeps the first expression’s type. NULLIF(value, 0) can guard a division by zero.

topics.title: Implicit conversion: the silent performance killer
topics.detail: Match parameter types to column types. Comparing a VARCHAR employee code to an INT may convert the indexed column, affect index use, and fail for nonnumeric codes.

topics.title: Chapter summary
topics.detail: Test missing rows and actual NULL values separately. A missing payroll entry, an unknown amount, and a recorded zero can have different business meanings.

topics.title: SELECT and projection
topics.detail: Project the columns the consumer needs, such as employee ID and name. A narrow projection can reduce transfer and make an index cover the query.

topics.title: Filtering with WHERE
topics.detail: Filter active employees with WHERE active = 1. Use half-open date intervals like work_date >= start AND work_date < next_start for reporting windows.

topics.title: Pattern matching
topics.detail: LIKE 'Ra%' matches a prefix and may use an index with compatible collation. A leading wildcard like '%afi' usually prevents an ordinary B-tree prefix seek.

topics.title: ORDER BY, TOP, and pagination
topics.detail: Use ORDER BY with a unique tie-breaker. T-SQL TOP (n) returns the first n rows under that ordering, while OFFSET/FETCH and cursor pagination model different browsing needs.

topics.title: CASE: conditional logic inside SQL
topics.detail: Use CASE to label shifts over a threshold or count approved leave conditionally. Include an ELSE when the report needs a default.

topics.title: INNER JOIN
topics.detail: An INNER JOIN from payroll to employees returns matched payroll components. Several components for one employee remain several output rows.

topics.title: LEFT JOIN and the WHERE trap
topics.detail: Place the optional table’s January filter in ON when all employees must remain visible. A WHERE comparison on the right-side date removes NULL-extended rows.

topics.title: Anti-joins: finding what is missing
topics.detail: Use NOT EXISTS to find active employees missing January payroll. The inner query tests for a matching employee and period.

topics.title: Self joins
topics.detail: Join employees to employees with different aliases to display each employee beside their manager. A LEFT JOIN preserves the CEO.

topics.title: CROSS JOIN and CROSS APPLY
topics.detail: CROSS JOIN produces every employee/day pair for a schedule. T-SQL CROSS APPLY evaluates a right-side table expression for each left row. OUTER APPLY preserves rows with no match.

topics.title: Join fan-out: the duplicate-money bug
topics.detail: Joining raw attendance and leave by employee multiplies each source’s facts. Sum each at employee grain before joining. The dashboard exercise demonstrates this.

topics.title: Physical join algorithms
topics.detail: Nested loops can suit small outer inputs with indexed lookups. Hash joins can suit larger equality joins. Merge joins can exploit matching sort order.

topics.title: The aggregate functions
topics.detail: COUNT measures rows, SUM totals values, AVG computes a mean, and MIN/MAX find extremes. AVG of shift lengths differs from AVG of employee-level totals.

topics.title: GROUP BY and the every-column rule
topics.detail: For portable grouping, put each selected nonaggregate expression in GROUP BY. SQL Server requires this where the expression references input columns.

topics.title: WHERE vs HAVING
topics.detail: WHERE filters shifts before grouping. HAVING SUM(minutes_worked) > 900 filters completed employee groups.

topics.title: Conditional aggregation
topics.detail: SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'approved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) counts only approved entries within each group.

topics.title: GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP, CUBE
topics.detail: In T-SQL, GROUPING SETS enumerates subtotal grains. ROLLUP follows a hierarchy and CUBE generates every combination. GROUPING distinguishes subtotal NULLs from stored NULLs.

topics.title: The four operators
topics.detail: UNION deduplicates, UNION ALL appends, INTERSECT returns common tuples, and EXCEPT returns distinct tuples from the left that are absent on the right.

topics.title: Rules and NULL behaviour
topics.detail: Align column positions and compatible types. Duplicate elimination treats NULLs in equivalent positions as equal. Add ORDER BY to the full compound query for deterministic output.

topics.title: Scalar, multi-valued, and correlated
topics.detail: A scalar subquery must yield at most one row in SQL Server. IN accepts a set. A correlated subquery refers to the outer row and can often be expressed as a join or grouped aggregate.

topics.title: EXISTS vs IN vs JOIN
topics.detail: Use EXISTS for employee membership without multiplying rows. JOIN is appropriate when columns from the matched table are needed and its grain is intentional.

topics.title: The NOT IN NULL trap
topics.detail: If an IN list can contain NULL, NOT IN can evaluate to UNKNOWN even when no equality match exists. A correlated NOT EXISTS avoids the trap for nonnullable employee IDs.

topics.title: Derived tables
topics.detail: A derived table is a subquery in FROM. Give it an alias and use it to expose a computed total to an outer filter or join.

topics.title: Why CTEs
topics.detail: Use a named CTE to explain query stages such as employee totals followed by payroll rank. A CTE does not promise a cached result.

topics.title: Recursive CTEs
topics.detail: Start with an anchor then UNION ALL a recursive member. Track visited nodes or cap depth, and use SQL Server MAXRECURSION as an execution guard.

topics.title: Generating a series
topics.detail: A recursive CTE can build a short calendar. For frequently used calendars, use a permanent date dimension or GENERATE_SERIES on supported SQL Server versions and compatibility levels.

topics.title: Updatable CTEs
topics.detail: SQL Server can update through some CTEs that map to an updatable base table. Preview target IDs and verify that joins identify each target row once.

topics.title: The anatomy of OVER
topics.detail: OVER defines a partition, an order, and where supported a frame. Payroll ranks can restart in each department without collapsing rows.

topics.title: Ranking functions
topics.detail: ROW_NUMBER assigns a unique sequence, RANK leaves gaps for ties, and DENSE_RANK counts distinct ordered values. Match the function to the business rule.

topics.title: Top-N per group
topics.detail: Compute the rank in a CTE and filter it in the outer query. Rank by pay alone if tied employees must share a position.

topics.title: Offset functions: LAG and LEAD
topics.detail: LAG reads a preceding row and LEAD a following row. Generate missing calendar periods first when a report needs the previous calendar month.

topics.title: Frames: ROWS vs RANGE
topics.detail: ROWS advances by physical rows under the window order. RANGE can include all peers at the same sort value. Use a stable tie-breaker for per-entry running totals.

topics.title: The gaps-and-islands problem
topics.detail: Deduplicate attendance dates, subtract their sequence number from the day number, and group equal differences to find consecutive runs.

chapters.title: Views, Temp Tables, and Table Variables

topics.title: Views
topics.detail: A view provides a named SELECT, such as an active roster. Filter and order the outer query according to the caller’s needs.

topics.title: Indexed (materialised) views
topics.detail: A SQL Server indexed view persists its result using a unique clustered index. Eligibility rules include schema binding and required SET options. Check write overhead.

topics.title: Temp tables vs table variables
topics.detail: Use a #temp table to stage a larger intermediate result with statistics and indexes. A table variable can suit small scopes. Deferred compilation can help estimates on supported SQL Server versions.

topics.title: INSERT patterns
topics.detail: Name target columns explicitly. Use INSERT SELECT for a set of rows and SQL Server OUTPUT when the caller needs inserted IDs.

topics.title: UPDATE with a join
topics.detail: Update from a source whose join yields at most one row per employee. A duplicate source makes UPDATE FROM nondeterministic in SQL Server.

topics.title: DELETE, TRUNCATE, and batching
topics.detail: DELETE can filter rows and fire delete triggers. SQL Server TRUNCATE clears the whole table under stricter rules and resets identity. For large selective deletes, commit bounded batches.

topics.title: MERGE / UPSERT
topics.detail: Enforce a unique business key first. Review SQL Server MERGE concurrency and version behavior, or use transactional update/insert. SQLite supports ON CONFLICT on a unique key.

topics.title: The transfer that must not lose money
topics.detail: Move a payroll adjustment between ledger rows in one transaction. Validate both row counts and roll back all changes on failure so the total stays balanced.

topics.title: The four concurrency phenomena
topics.detail: Dirty reads see uncommitted changes. Nonrepeatable reads see a row change, phantoms see membership change, and lost updates overwrite another writer’s work.

topics.title: Isolation levels
topics.detail: Compare READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SNAPSHOT, and SERIALIZABLE with two sessions. SQL Server READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT changes how READ COMMITTED reads are served.

topics.title: Optimistic vs pessimistic concurrency
topics.detail: An optimistic update checks a version token in WHERE and detects zero rows affected. A pessimistic workflow takes locks before making a decision. Keep either transaction short.

topics.title: Deadlocks
topics.detail: Deadlocks are lock cycles. Inspect the deadlock graph, use a consistent access order, and retry SQL Server error 1205 with bounded attempts for retry-safe operations.

topics.title: Anatomy of a production procedure
topics.detail: A production procedure declares typed parameters, validates inputs, uses SET NOCOUNT ON, and defines its transaction and error contract.

topics.title: Why procedures still matter in an ORM world
topics.detail: A procedure can package a multi-step payroll operation behind one call and scoped permissions. Keep simple ORM queries when they fit the use case.

topics.title: Scalar functions: the performance trap
topics.detail: A scalar UDF can be invoked per row and hide work. SQL Server may inline eligible functions on supported versions. Confirm the compiled plan.

topics.title: Inline table-valued functions: the good kind
topics.detail: An inline TVF is a parameterized relational expression. An attendance TVF using a single SELECT can be joined to the roster by the caller.

topics.title: Table-valued parameters
topics.detail: Pass a batch of employee IDs using a READONLY table-valued parameter. SQL Server does not maintain column statistics on TVPs, so consider staging a large batch.

topics.title: An audit trigger
topics.detail: Use inserted and deleted as sets in SQL Server. Join by employee ID to write one audit entry per changed employee, including multi-row updates.

topics.title: INSTEAD OF triggers
topics.detail: An INSTEAD OF trigger replaces the original operation. On a view, it can direct allowed inserts into underlying tables and enforce a clear write contract.

topics.title: When not to use a trigger
topics.detail: Prefer declarative constraints for integrity and explicit transactions for side effects callers need to understand. Triggers run on the writer’s path and need multi-row tests.

chapters.title: Loops, Cursors, and Thinking in Sets

topics.title: Why loops are slow here
topics.detail: Row-at-a-time processing repeats work and may increase round trips. A grouped payroll query lets the engine plan one relational operation.

topics.title: The cursor: full syntax, so you can read legacy code
topics.detail: Recognize DECLARE CURSOR, OPEN, FETCH, the @@FETCH_STATUS loop, CLOSE, and DEALLOCATE when maintaining legacy T-SQL.

topics.title: The same thing, set-based
topics.detail: Replace per-employee totals with GROUP BY employee_id, and per-row labels with CASE. Compare outputs including employees with no facts.

topics.title: The set-based translation table
topics.detail: Common translations include counters to COUNT, running totals to SUM OVER, per-row membership checks to EXISTS, and next-row comparisons to LEAD.

topics.title: The WHILE loop and when loops are actually right
topics.detail: A WHILE loop can manage bounded cleanup batches or retry transient failures. Use a terminating condition and keep work inside each batch set-based.

topics.title: RBAR, and where it hides in application code
topics.detail: ORM navigation access can cause one query per employee. Count database commands and batch fetch explicit projections for the page.

topics.title: The right way and the catastrophic way
topics.detail: Keep SQL structure fixed where possible. When structure must vary in SQL Server, use sp_executesql with typed parameters for employee and date values.

topics.title: Identifiers cannot be parameters
topics.detail: Bind values as parameters. For dynamic sort columns, map a user selection to a fixed allowlist and quote approved identifiers with QUOTENAME.

topics.title: The optional-parameter problem
topics.detail: A shared optional-filter expression can produce weak plans across selective and broad calls. Compare parameterized branches, recompilation, or version-supported optimization after measuring.

topics.title: TRY/CATCH and what it does not catch
topics.detail: Wrap the transaction in TRY/CATCH. Same-scope compilation errors and connection termination can escape CATCH. Validate failure behavior in a test database.

topics.title: THROW vs RAISERROR
topics.detail: Use THROW inside CATCH to rethrow the original error. RAISERROR has older formatting and severity controls and does not honor SET XACT_ABORT.

topics.title: Nested transactions are a lie
topics.detail: An inner COMMIT only decrements @@TRANCOUNT. Coordinate ownership with callers, use savepoints where valid, and check XACT_STATE before deciding how to roll back.

topics.title: STRING_AGG and STRING_SPLIT
topics.detail: Use STRING_AGG with explicit ordering when order matters. STRING_SPLIT returns rows; on supported versions request ordinal and order by it to restore input order.

topics.title: Dates done right
topics.detail: Use typed boundaries and compare the stored date or timestamp directly. Define the business time zone before deriving a calendar day and test daylight-saving transitions for timestamps.

topics.title: JSON
topics.detail: Use SQL Server JSON_VALUE for scalars and OPENJSON for arrays or typed rowsets. Validate shape and retain relational keys for frequently joined data.

topics.title: PIVOT
topics.detail: T-SQL PIVOT turns known status values into columns. Conditional aggregation is a portable alternative that also makes zero-handling explicit.

topics.title: The B-tree
topics.detail: B-tree indexes support ordered traversal and range access. Inspect both scan and search plans on the same attendance filter.

topics.title: Clustered vs nonclustered
topics.detail: A clustered index organizes SQL Server rowstore data at its leaf. A nonclustered index has a separate structure and uses a row locator to reach the base row.

topics.title: Composite keys: order is everything
topics.detail: Key order follows the workload. For WHERE employee_id = ? AND work_date >= ?, an employee/date index enables an equality prefix and a date range.

topics.title: Covering indexes and INCLUDE
topics.detail: Use T-SQL INCLUDE for columns required only as payload. SQLite can cover queries by storing payload as additional index key columns.

topics.title: Filtered indexes
topics.detail: A SQL Server filtered index can target approved leave. The predicate must align with the query. SQLite calls this a partial index.

topics.title: The cost of an index
topics.detail: Indexes consume storage and add work to writes. Compare payroll import throughput and report reads before keeping an index.

topics.title: Finding missing and unused indexes
topics.detail: Review missing-index and usage DMVs alongside actual plans. Account for restarts and reporting cycles. Consolidate overlapping indexes only after checking key order, includes, and workload.

topics.title: Cardinality estimation is the whole ballgame
topics.detail: Estimated row counts influence join types and memory grants. Compare estimates to actual rows for a heavily populated department and a rare one.

topics.title: When statistics go stale
topics.detail: After bulk changes, check stats freshness and sample quality with SQL Server statistics metadata. Test a targeted update rather than refreshing every index blindly.

topics.title: Where estimates go wrong
topics.detail: Correlated predicates, skew, stale histograms, and opaque expressions can distort estimates. Investigate the earliest significant mismatch and test one change.

chapters.title: Execution Plans, SARGability, and Parameter Sniffing

topics.title: Reading a plan
topics.detail: In an actual SQL Server execution plan, inspect row counts, residual predicates, repeated lookups, joins, sorts, and spills. A scan can be appropriate for broad queries.

topics.title: SARGability
topics.detail: Keep filters search-argument friendly. Replace a month function on work_date with a half-open range, then compare logical reads.

topics.title: Parameter sniffing
topics.detail: SQL Server can compile with one set of parameter values and reuse the resulting plan. Compare common and rare values and evaluate Query Store evidence before changing plan policy.

topics.title: Query Store
topics.detail: Query Store records historical query text, plan versions, and runtime statistics. Use it to compare deployments and time windows or investigate regressions.

topics.title: Case 1: The date function scan
topics.detail: Compare the attendance date-function filter against a range under the same index. Verify that February 1 is excluded in both plans.

topics.title: Case 2: The correlated subquery in the SELECT list
topics.detail: Rewrite repeated correlated totals as a grouped relation joined once. An indexed lookup may still win for a selective outer input, so measure both.

topics.title: Case 3: The implicit conversion
topics.detail: Align employee code parameter types with column types. Check the actual plan for CONVERT_IMPLICIT on the indexed side and compare reads.

topics.title: Case 4: The N+1 endpoint
topics.detail: Fetch all attendance totals for an employee page with a single grouped query. Measure database command count and endpoint latency.

topics.title: Case 5: The OFFSET death march
topics.detail: Compare a deep OFFSET with a cursor containing pay_date and id. Include a tie on the page boundary and verify both pages return the same IDs.

topics.title: Case 6: The over-indexed table
topics.detail: Inventory overlapping payroll indexes. Measure import and report performance before and after consolidating one candidate in a test environment.

topics.title: The tuning method
topics.detail: Baseline reads and plans, define expected rows, change one element, and repeat with representative parameter values. Keep the change only if correctness and the measured workload support it.

topics.title: Normal forms, practically
topics.detail: Model repeating shifts as rows, ensure attributes depend on the full key, and store department attributes with their own key when multiple employees share them.

topics.title: Denormalize deliberately, or not at all
topics.detail: If dashboard totals justify a summary table, define the refresh cadence, staleness contract, owner, and reconciliation query.

topics.title: The anti-pattern catalogue
topics.detail: Review how the following designs change constraint enforcement and query shape for an HR system.

topics.title: Entity-Attribute-Value
topics.detail: An EAV model makes typed filters and constraints harder to express. Put frequently queried HR attributes in typed columns and reserve flexible metadata for genuine extension points.

topics.title: Comma-separated values in a column
topics.detail: Replace comma-separated role IDs with an employee_role table keyed by employee_id and role_id. This enables foreign keys and ordinary joins.

topics.title: Polymorphic associations
topics.detail: A generic target_type and target_id pair cannot use one ordinary foreign key to several targets. Consider separate relationship tables or a shared parent entity.

topics.title: The god table
topics.detail: Split a wide employee/payroll/leave table by entity and lifecycle. Use joins and views to reconstruct specific report projections.

topics.title: Storing money as FLOAT, and dates as strings
topics.detail: Use exact numeric money and native SQL Server dates. The SQLite fixture uses integer cents and ISO dates because its type system differs.

topics.title: No foreign keys “for performance”
topics.detail: Preserve relationship integrity with foreign keys. Index relevant child keys based on the join and delete workload.

topics.title: Practical design rules
topics.detail: Choose a row grain, enforce its natural uniqueness, test foreign key paths, and measure before adding indexes or redundant fields.

topics.title: The questions, and what they are really testing
topics.detail: Explain your expected output, edge cases, access path, and evidence. Practice justifying DENSE_RANK for ties and a bounded retry for deadlocks.

topics.title: Exercises
topics.detail: Translate the PDF drills to HRMS: zero-count departments, ranked payroll, rolling attendance activity, running balances, missing activity, manager chain, streaks, and month-over-month totals.

topics.title: Selected solutions
topics.detail: Start with the exact grain for each drill. Use LEFT JOIN for zeroes, window ranks for top totals, a date range for rolling activity, SUM OVER for running totals, NOT EXISTS for absent activity, recursion for the chain, and a calendar plus LAG for month-over-month growth.

topics.title: What to study next
topics.detail: Explore date-based partitioning, columnstore analytics, system-versioned temporal HR records, memory-optimized tables for measured bottlenecks, and isolation guarantees across service boundaries.
